papers.title: Shox2 maintains thalamocortical neuron firing for whisker-based somatomotor responses and sleep spindles in mice
papers.abstract: In the mouse thalamus, thalamocortical neurons (TCNs) relay sensory information to cortex and generate rhythmic activity, including sleep spindles, through precisely timed firing. TCNs switch between tonic and burst firing modes that depend on intrinsic membrane properties, yet what maintains these properties in the mature thalamus remains unknown. Transcription factors, which regulate the ion channel genes that shape firing, are natural candidates. Here, we investigate Shox2, a transcription factor implicated in rhythmic activity across multiple systems, in ventral posterior medial (VPM) thalamus. Using genetic labeling and optogenetic activation, we show that Shox2 expressing neurons form functional thalamocortical and thalamoreticular projections capable of driving cortical responses. Conditional knockout of Shox2 in VPM alters intrinsic membrane properties, reducing both tonic and burst firing without altering thalamocortical circuit organization or barrel field architecture. These firing deficits are accompanied by impaired whisker-dependent somatomotor performance and a reduction in sleep spindle density in cortical target regions, while overall sleep architecture remains intact. Together, these findings identify Shox2 as a transcriptional regulator required to maintain intrinsic firing modes in VPM thalamocortical neurons, linking a transcription factor to spindle deficits, an emerging neurophysiological biomarker for autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia.

Shox2 loss impaired whisker-dependent somatomotor performance and reduced cortical sleep spindle density, identifying a transcriptional regulator linking firing modes to spindle deficits.

papers.title: WakeSentry: real-time awakening detection from single-channel EEG across sleep cohorts and forehead headbands
papers.abstract: Objective/Background: Awakenings after sleep onset are a core measure of sleep continuity, and EEG headbands and closed-loop stimulators, now used at home, must detect each one as it happens, to count it or to stop stimulation. Open sleep stagers match expert scorers, yet have been evaluated only offline over whole nights, so their real-time performance is untested. Patients/Methods: To fill this gap, we developed WakeSentry, which reads only past frontal EEG and learns the moment of waking through an awakening module. We tested it on 1,529 nights from five polysomnography (PSG) cohorts, three clinical, each held out of training, and on 224 headband nights, against GSSC, U-Sleep and YASA. Results: At a matched rate of 0.5 false awakenings per hour, WakeSentry caught more awakenings than GSSC in every cohort and on both headbands. On PSG its sensitivity rose from 63.8% to 70.5%, above U-Sleep and YASA on average. On the headbands it rose from 49.8% to 53.9%, a gain lost without the awakening module. With thresholds preset on the training cohorts, it still outperformed GSSC in six of seven test sets, with at most 0.40 false awakenings per hour. As a replayed stimulator gate, it shortened stimulation during wake in five test sets while staying open for at least 85% of N2 and N3. Conclusions: WakeSentry therefore works in patients and on unseen headbands. It can count awakenings at home and stop stimulation at each one, enabling multi-night monitoring of insomnia and closed-loop stimulation that stops when the sleeper wakes.

papers.title: NED-Net: open-source software for building and refining seizure detectors during rodent EEG experiments
papers.abstract: Long-term EEG is the main readout of rodent epilepsy models, and automated detectors are usually delivered as fixed models that a laboratory cannot adapt to its own animals. NED-Net is open-source software in which annotations, rule-based detections and model proposals share one file per recording, reviewed events train the next detector, and detection runs live during acquisition, so a detector can be refined while an experiment runs. A detector built in NED-Net on one kainate mouse cohort detected 64% of 221 video-adjudicated convulsive seizures in a second cohort as delivered, and 72% of its detections on held-out recordings were seizures. Retraining on annotations made in the app, a few seconds of review per event, raised recall to 88% at 74% precision. SeizyML, a published detector, reached similar recall with three times the detections and did not improve with the same annotations. A convulsive classifier removes non-seizures and enriches convulsive events.

papers.title: Nsun5 deficiency leads to impaired myelin integrity and sleep disruption.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption is common in disorders involving white-matter abnormalities, but the molecular pathways linking ribosomal RNA modification to disordered sleep remain unclear. NSUN5, which encodes an rRNA methyltransferase, is deleted in most patients with Williams-Beuren syndrome (WBS), a condition frequently accompanied by sleep problems. This clinical association suggests that loss of NSUN5 may contribute to sleep dysfunction, potentially through mechanisms relevant to white-matter integrity and neural activity. We combined electroencephalography/electromyography phenotyping, transcriptomics, ribosome profiling, nascent proteomics, proteomics, electron microscopy, positron emission tomography-computed tomography, and pharmacological rescue experiments in Nsun5-knockout mice to define how loss of Nsun5-dependent 28 S ribosomal RNA 5-methylcytosine affects white-matter integrity and sleep. Nsun5 deficiency markedly reduced 28 S rRNA m5C levels and led to selective translational dysregulation rather than global translational failure. The affected translational programs were enriched in myelination-related pathways and voltage-gated potassium channel subunits, including Kcna1 and Kcna2. At the cellular and tissue levels, these alterations were associated with oligodendrocyte loss, diffuse hypomyelination of the corpus callosum, and increased regional cortical metabolic activity. Correspondingly, Nsun5-knockout mice exhibited reduced non-rapid-eye-movement sleep and altered nocturnal sleep organization. Treatment with clemastine significantly improved sleep abnormalities and restored myelin integrity, while treatment with 4-aminopyridine also alleviated the sleep phenotype. These findings suggest that Nsun5-dependent rRNA methylation contributes to sleep disruption in association with white-matter dysfunction and altered potassium-channel-related protein abundance. Our results provide a preclinical framework for understanding sleep disturbances associated with WBS and other myelin-related neurological conditions.

Clemastine improved sleep abnormalities and myelin integrity, and 4-aminopyridine also alleviated the sleep phenotype, linking rRNA methylation to white-matter dysfunction and sleep disruption.

papers.title: Targeting memory consolidation in major depression via pharmacological slow-wave sleep promotion
papers.abstract: Slow-wave sleep (SWS) has been implicated in memory consolidation and brain plasticity and proposed as a therapeutic target in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, whether pharmacological promotion of SWS causally improves memory consolidation remains unknown. Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a robust enhancer of SWS, represents a promising drug-repurposing candidate to target this pathway. We therefore conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 22 patients with MDD and 20 matched healthy controls receiving single nocturnal doses of GHB, trazodone as an active comparator, or placebo under polysomnographic monitoring (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04082806). Declarative, procedural and emotional memory were assessed before and after sleep. GHB strongly increased SWS duration and delta power, whereas trazodone produced smaller changes in sleep-stage composition. Contrary to our hypothesis, neither drug improved memory consolidation across domains. Exploratory analyses revealed weak associations between global sleep-stage measures and memory, alongside selective associations with spindle and spectral features. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing SWS alone is sufficient to improve overnight memory consolidation and suggest that more targeted modulation of sleep oscillatory dynamics may be required.

papers.title: MLE EEG Toolbox: A Personal AI Laboratory Assistant for Literature-Informed and Reproducible M/EEG Research
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological research increasingly relies on complex analytical workflows, yet integrating methodological evidence, computational execution and reproducibility remains challenging. Here we introduce MLE EEG Toolbox, a framework for building a personal AI laboratory assistant for electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) research. The toolbox integrates locally deployed AI, natural-language-guided analysis, literature retrieval and methodological comparison, and reproducible computational workflows. A constrained language model translates research instructions into validated, researcher-approved operations, while literature-informed guidance supports parameter selection and protocol reconstruction. Computational provenance enables transparent inspection and replay of analytical workflows. The assistant achieved action-selection accuracies of 85.6% for EEG and 95.5% for MEG, while 142 cross-platform tests demonstrated close numerical agreement. Applications to public EEG and MEG datasets illustrated integrated spectral, network, decoding and source analyses. Running on standard personal computers without external AI APIs or token charges, MLE EEG Toolbox provides an accessible, researcher-controlled environment that connects methodological knowledge with reproducible electrophysiological analysis.

papers.title: A Soft Sponge-Pillar Electrode Platform for Motion-Tolerant Ambulatory EEG and Sleep Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiological recording systems are essential for both clinical and real-world environments. While a wide range of wearable devices have been reported for electrocardiogram (ECG) and electromyogram (EMG) recording applications, most electroencephalography (EEG) measurements still require subjects to remain stationary while wearing rigid and uncomfortable equipment. Here, a soft and wearable sponge pillar EEG electrode is presented for long-term and motion-tolerant EEG recording. The electrode is composed of two layers of a carbon black (CB)-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composite, where a firmer solid base assists in bypassing hair, enabling stable access to the scalp, while a porous sponge tip ensures comfort, reliable contact, and low skin-electrode impedance. Fabricated via a sugar templating process without microfabrication steps, the microporous sponge structure offers low modulus and significantly enhances the contact area with the skin when loaded with conductive gel. This allows the electrode to achieve a lower contact impedance of $1.62 \times 10^{4}\,Ω$ at 10 Hz, outperforming conventional gelled electrodes while maintaining gel stability for over 18 hours. With the electrodes integrated into wearable form factors such as headbands, headphones, and baseball caps, EEG signal recording during motion have been demonstrated, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 16.46 dB. These features establish the sponge pillar electrode as a promising platform for next generation wearable EEG systems, enabling comfortable, stable, and prolonged brain signal acquisition on ambulatory subjects and in naturalistic environments.

It achieved 1.62×10^4 Ω contact impedance at 10 Hz with gel stability over 18 h and recorded EEG during motion (headbands, headphones, caps) at 16.46 dB SNR.

papers.title: Sleep-Deprivation Serum Induces Mitochondrial Stress in BV2 Cells: Responses to P2Y12-Targeted Pharmacological Modulation.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) disrupts neuroimmune and metabolic homeostasis, but whether circulating factors generated after sleep loss alter microglial responses to purinergic pharmacological modulation remains unclear. P2Y12 is a microglia-enriched purinergic receptor that regulates process dynamics, calcium signaling, and microglial interactions with neurons and vascular-glial interfaces. Here, we established an in vitro serum-transfer model to test whether serum from sleep-deprived mice alters mitochondrial and Rhod-2 fluorescence responses to P2Y12-targeted compounds in BV2 cells. Mice were subjected to forced-wheel SD consisting of one wheel revolution every 2 s for 4 h per day over 4 consecutive days, and serum was obtained by cardiac blood collection followed by centrifugation. BV2 cells were treated with control or SD serum in the absence or presence of the P2Y12 antagonist MRS2395 or the P2Y12 agonist 2-MeSADP. Mitochondrial membrane potential was assessed by JC-1 red/green ratio imaging, mitochondrial network integrity by MitoTracker-based segmentation and skeletonization, and Rhod-2 fluorescence responses by single-cell F/F0 imaging. SD serum decreased the JC-1 ratio, increased maximal depolarization, reduced mitochondrial skeleton length and mitochondrial area fraction, and suppressed Rhod-2 responses. Under control-serum conditions, MRS2395 markedly enhanced Rhod-2 responses, whereas the increase in the area under the Rhod-2 response curve with 2-MeSADP was not significant after Holm correction. Under SD-serum conditions, however, neither compound consistently restored the mitochondrial or Rhod-2 response profile. Together, these findings link SD-serum exposure to mitochondrial impairment and attenuated Rhod-2 fluorescence responses in BV2 cells, and suggest that serum context may influence cellular responses to P2Y12-targeted compounds.

papers.title: Psychedelics and Sleep: Preclinical and Human Studies-A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Background: Classic psychedelics, including LSD, psilocybin, and N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT)/ayahuasca, have shown promise as rapid-acting treatments for psychiatric disorders. Because sleep plays a central role in emotional regulation and neuroplasticity, psychedelic-induced changes in sleep architecture are of interest. Methods: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed was searched for preclinical and clinical studies published up to May 1, 2026, investigating psychedelics and sleep-related outcomes. Twelve eligible studies evaluated LSD, psilocybin, or DMT/ayahuasca and assessed sleep architecture, sleep quality, electroencephalographic activity, or dreams. Study validity was assessed using appropriate methodological tools. Results: Preclinical studies consistently demonstrated acute REM sleep suppression, delayed REM onset, increased wakefulness, and transient disruption of non-REM sleep. Human findings were more heterogeneous, although randomized trials reported prolonged REM latency after psilocybin and reduced REM duration after ayahuasca. Evidence regarding slow-wave activity (SWA) was mixed, with ayahuasca increasing early-cycle SWA and psilocybin reducing absolute delta power during the first sleep cycle. Subjective sleep quality showed little acute change in controlled trials, whereas one large naturalistic study reported reductions in sleep disturbances following psilocybin. Administration close to bedtime appeared more disruptive than daytime dosing. In general, quality assessments indicated fair-to-poor validity and notable risk of bias. Conclusions: Classic psychedelics produce acute but transient alterations in sleep physiology, particularly affecting REM sleep. Whether these changes contribute to therapeutic effects remains uncertain. Larger, well-controlled studies using standardized polysomnographic methods are needed to clarify the relationship between psychedelic-induced sleep modulation and clinical outcomes. This review was not prospectively registered.

ai.reason: Review of psychedelic effects on REM/NREM and SWA; some mechanistic sleep-architecture interest but peripheral to homeostasis research.
ai.summary: This PRISMA-guided systematic review of 12 preclinical and clinical studies found that classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT/ayahuasca) consistently produce acute REM sleep suppression, delayed REM onset, and increased wakefulness in preclinical work, with heterogeneous human findings including prolonged REM latency after psilocybin and reduced REM duration after ayahuasca. Evidence on slow-wave activity was mixed, and included studies showed fair-to-poor validity and notable risk of bias.

papers.title: Spikes in the night: rapid eye movement sleep maximally attenuates epileptiform spike morphology.
papers.abstract: To characterize morphological differences in interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) across sleep-wake states (rapid eye movement (REM), Non-REM1-3, wakefulness). Prospectively analyzed 7379 IEDs from 17 adults with focal epilepsy (12 unifocal, 5 multifocal) admitted to an epilepsy monitoring unit for continuous surface video-EEG telemetry (41.8±17.2 years, 52.9% females) using custom-developed software allowing manual confirmation of IEDs and sleep-wake states. Nine morphological IED features reflecting paroxysmal depolarizing shift dynamics and magnitude were quantified across three EEG montages (raw, referential and Laplacian). Nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis and post hoc Dunn-Sidak tests with Bonferroni correction assessed state-dependent differences. Only features surviving correction across all montages were considered reproducibly significant. IED morphology varied significantly by state (p < 10-12-10-134). Across all montages and subgroups, REM IEDs had shallowest slopes (upslope 2.91-4.22 μV/s; downslope 2.87-4.33 μV/s), bluntest peaks (27.04°-40.24°), and shortest amplitudes and smallest area, (multifocal-driven). Awake IEDs had steepest slopes (upslope 8.97-15.23 μV/s; downslope 7.54-13.84 μV/s), and spikiest peaks (8.18°-14.44°). NREM IEDs were intermediate. Epileptiform morphology in REM was most attenuated. Shallower slopes, blunter peaks, shorter, and smaller-area IEDs indicate an electrobiological milieu less promoting of epileptic activity than NREM's synchronized state or wakefulness's maximally responsive state. Despite REM and wakefulness being desynchronized on surface EEG, REM's morphological IED divergence raises future directions into sui generis anti-epileptic mechanisms, including network connectivity and pH-responsive orexinergic glial dynamics. The sleep-wake cycle strongly modulates epileptic activity, yet seizures rarely arise from REM (~1%). However, REM contains sufficient IEDs to characterize morphology and probe potential anti-epileptic solutions via their underlying cellular mechanisms.

papers.title: Circadian modulation of dopamine release shapes reward-evoked signaling in the nucleus accumbens.
papers.abstract: The circadian system is an important regulator of reward-related neural function and behavior. Dopamine (DA) release in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) is a key component of reward processing, yet how circadian timing shapes DA release in relation to reward behavior remains unclear. Here, we investigated circadian rhythms in DA release and reward behavior in C57BL/6J mice expressing the genetically encoded DA sensor DA3m in the NAc using long-term fiber photometry paired with an automated reward delivery and measurement system. Spontaneous DA, reflecting broad changes in DA release during natural behavior, peaked during the early subjective day. In a separate group of mice, targeted disruption of the molecular clock gene Bmal1 in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) strongly attenuated spontaneous DA rhythmicity, supporting a role for the SCN molecular clock in regulating these rhythms. Reward-evoked DA peaked during the day-to-night transition, while cue-evoked DA and reward behavior peaked during the early subjective night. Linear mixed-effects modeling showed that reward-evoked DA was positively associated with reward behavior and cue-evoked DA but negatively associated with baseline DA measured immediately before reward availability. Reward-evoked DA differed across circadian time even after accounting for reward behavior or cue-evoked DA, while higher baseline DA predicted smaller reward-evoked responses and the strength of this relationship also changed across circadian time. Together, these findings show that circadian time changes both the magnitude of reward-evoked DA responses and how those responses relate to baseline and cue-evoked dopamine signaling and reward behavior.

SCN-specific Bmal1 disruption attenuated spontaneous dopamine rhythmicity, and reward-evoked dopamine was positively associated with reward behavior and cue-evoked dopamine but negatively associated with pre-reward baseline dopamine.

papers.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
papers.abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3–96.8% hold-out accuracy, and augmenting real clinical EEG with NeuroSim samples raised AD-vs-control accuracy from 91.6% to 94.5% and PD-vs-control from 90.9% to 94.0%.

papers.title: AI-Based Monitoring Devices for the Identification of Circadian Parameters as Digital Predictive Biomarkers of Neurodegenerative Diseases in Older Adults: Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and related dementias are a growing health burden among older adults. Circadian disruption is increasingly recognized as both a consequence and a potential early marker of neurodegenerative progression. Wearable sensing combined with AI enables continuous, noninvasive, and ecologically valid monitoring of circadian parameters as potential digital biomarkers. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on AI-enhanced wearable and objective sensing devices used to monitor circadian parameters in older and cognitively vulnerable adults and evaluates their potential as digital predictive biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases. Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines, an original search of PubMed, Scopus, and JMIR journals (June 2025) yielded 12 studies, 7 of which met updated eligibility criteria on rescreening. A complementary search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library (March 24, 2026) added 3 eligible studies and 3 sensitivity references (excluded records retained to delimit the corpus boundary). Two reviewers (JMH-Z and JM-R) independently assessed risk of bias with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Heterogeneous end points precluded meta-analysis; the narrative synthesis covered 4 prespecified domains: device class, circadian construct, AI and machine learning (ML) method family, and population and neurocognitive context. The final corpus comprised 13 records (10 eligible studies and 3 sensitivity references) published from 2015 to 2025. Wrist actigraphy predominated, and samples ranged from community-dwelling older adults to nursing home residents with advanced dementia (n=16-7297). Circadian parameters included interdaily stability, intradaily variability, relative amplitude, midline estimating statistic of rhythm, acrophase, and circadian stimulus. AI/ML methods included supervised learning (random forests, gradient boosting, and regression models), unsupervised clustering, and algorithm development or validation; 7 studies applied deterministic algorithms without fitting a predictive model. Circadian fragmentation was associated with functional decline, dementia risk, and cognitive performance. Most studies were descriptive or observational with small, nondiverse samples; no AI model was externally validated, and no study followed an AI-specific reporting guideline. AI-enhanced wearable devices show meaningful potential for noninvasive measurement of circadian disruption in older and cognitively vulnerable populations. Evidence certainty is moderate for actigraphy-derived fragmentation-function associations in institutional settings and low for predictive biomarker claims in community populations. From 6 recurring challenges along the sensing-to-biomarker pipeline, we propose a 4-layer reference architecture (sensing and acquisition, circadian parameter extraction, AI/ML inference, and a clinical and validation interface) with a layered validation pathway. Longitudinal, multisite validation studies using standardized circadian metrics, diverse populations, and explainable AI remain necessary before clinical deployment as neurodegenerative biomarkers.

ai.summary: This PRISMA-2020 systematic review synthesized 13 records (10 eligible studies, 2015-2025) on AI-enhanced wearable and objective sensing of circadian parameters as digital predictive biomarkers in older and cognitively vulnerable adults, mostly wrist actigraphy, with heterogeneous endpoints precluding meta-analysis. Circadian fragmentation was associated with functional decline, dementia risk, and cognitive performance, but no AI model was externally validated; certainty was moderate for actigraphy-fragmentation associations in institutional settings and low for community predictive biomarker claims, and a 4-layer reference architecture with a layered validation pathway was proposed.

papers.title: Two Axes of Sleep, One Heart: Dissociating Objective Sleep-Disordered Breathing From Subjective Sleep Duration in Cardiac Risk
papers.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular epidemiology has long treated "sleep" as a single exposure, although it denotes both an objective physiological state and a subjective behaviour. We tested whether these domains carry separable information about cardiac risk. Methods and Results: We derived an objective axis from 8,444 polysomnograms (Sleep Heart Health Study) and a subjective axis of self-reported duration from 407,303 adults in the 2020 and 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. Multivariable regression (n=213,489), quadratic dose-response modelling, sleep-stratified comorbidity networks, and era-stratified tests were combined. Objective sleep-disordered breathing was continuous and right-skewed (median apnea-hypopnea index, 31.8 events/h; median sleep efficiency, 69%) in a risk-enriched cohort. Both short (<7 h) and long (>9 h) sleep were associated with disease after full adjustment: adjusted odds ratios for heart attack were 1.24 (95% CI, 1.19-1.30) and 1.30 (1.19-1.42), and for stroke 1.12 (1.06-1.17) and 1.42 (1.29-1.57). A positive quadratic term confirmed a U shape for all 4 outcomes formally tested (P[≤]6.3x102), with fitted nadirs of 7.26 to 7.85 hours. Suboptimal sleep also raised comorbidity-network density from 0.089 to 0.112 (short sleep; +26%) and 0.108 (long sleep; +22%), with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs and concordant effects across demographic strata. A survey-weighted replication in official CDC microdata (n=344,010; median design effect, 4.43) preserved the principal cardiac, U-shaped, and network findings; an exploratory COVID-19 interaction (P=0.020) did not survive design-based correction. Conclusions: Objective breathing pathology and subjective duration are separately prognostic, and suboptimal sleep amplifies the cardiometabolic comorbidity network. Duration alone cannot exclude asymptomatic sleep-disordered breathing; cardiovascular prevention should assess both axes.

ai.summary: Tested whether objective sleep-disordered breathing (8,444 polysomnograms) and subjective sleep duration (407,303 BRFSS adults) carry separable cardiac risk information using regression, dose-response, and comorbidity-network analyses. Both short (<7 h) and long (>9 h) sleep were associated with heart attack (AORs 1.24 and 1.30) and stroke (1.12 and 1.42), with U-shaped dose-response and increased comorbidity-network density under suboptimal sleep.

papers.title: Influence of social housing on dim light at night induced behavioural and hepatic alterations in mice.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption induced by dim light at night (DLAN) is increasingly recognised as an environmental stressor that adversely affects behavioural and metabolic physiology. While social interaction is known to buffer stress responses, whether it mitigates DLAN-induced behavioural and hepatic dysfunction remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study investigated the influence of social housing on behavioural, oxidative and hepatic alterations induced by chronic DLAN exposure in male mice. Sixty-four mice were assigned to four experimental groups comprising group-housed and socially isolated animals maintained under either a standard light-dark cycle or DLAN for 28 days. Behavioural assessments were performed to evaluate anxiety-like behaviour and anhedonia, followed by histological examination of the liver and biochemical analyses of antioxidant enzyme activities, glucose and hepatic function biomarkers. DLAN exposure increased anxiety-like behaviour, anhedonia, oxidative stress and hepatic dysfunction, with these effects being most pronounced in socially isolated mice. Histological analyses revealed marked hepatocellular degeneration and lipid accumulation in isolated DLAN-exposed animals, accompanied by reduced catalase and superoxide dismutase activities and elevated glucose, triglyceride and hepatic enzyme levels. In contrast, group-housed mice exposed to DLAN exhibited significantly attenuated behavioural deficits, improved antioxidant status and reduced hepatic injury compared with their socially isolated counterparts. These findings demonstrate that social housing alleviates DLAN-induced behavioural and hepatic dysfunction, highlighting the importance of social interaction as a modulator of physiological resilience during circadian disruption.

papers.title: Disentangling Monitor Hardware Artifacts and Smoothing Lag for Shift-Robust Intraoperative EEG and Hemodynamic Risk Calibration
papers.abstract: Commercial intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) and blood pressure monitors introduce cyclic impedance pulses, smoothing delays, direct-current (DC) drift, and cuff holds that confound risk forecasting and uncertainty calibration. We developed a causal signal-conditioning and shift-robust conformal calibration framework across 5,439 public anesthesia procedures. Streaming filters blank 10.13-min 64-Hz impedance checks, apply unclipped post-notch conditioning, separate 63-s suppression-ratio lag, and distinguish three-channel cuff inflations from dropouts across propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA; N = 3,214), volatile anesthesia (N = 2,046), European endoscopy sedation (N = 171), and DC-coupled surgery (N = 8). De-impedanced cortical tree ensembles were compared against deep sequence models, paired with patient-cluster Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted Conformal Risk Control (CRC) and lag-buffered online Conformal Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) tracking. Pre-filter blanking removed 97.90% and 97.60% of false flatline conflicts while preserving 99.23% and 98.96% of deep suppression. On unseen TIVA surgeries (N = 525), cortical features achieved area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) 0.3135 (1.94% prevalence) and 0.1627 (0.82% lag-free prevalence), with no detectable difference from deep encoders (p >= 0.36) and no cortical gain for hypotension (0.3432 vs. 0.3437, p = 0.784). Zero-retraining volatile transfer (N = 1,048) showed no detectable difference from an end-tidal gas oracle on lag-free suppression (0.0820 vs. 0.0736, p = 0.472). Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted CRC bounded all 70 TIVA shift cells at <= 4.38% (alpha = 5.0%) in 66.32 ms per 30-s epoch. Causal artifact disentangling and shift-aware conformal calibration support reliable real-time intraoperative risk bounds within explicit physiological observability limits.

papers.title: Frontal Low-Frequency Electroencephalographic Coherence in Bipolar Disorder: A Covariate-Controlled Secondary Analysis of a Public Resting-State EEG Feature Dataset.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo test whether bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with predefined frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp electroencephalography (EEG) coherence differences relative to healthy controls (HC), depressive disorder (DD), and schizophrenia (SZ) in a covariate-controlled reanalysis of a public resting-state EEG feature dataset.MethodsThe covariate-complete sample included 472 participants (93 HC, 66 BD, 196 DD, and 117 SZ). Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models adjusted for age, sex, education, and intelligence quotient (IQ). Primary outcomes were predefined frontal/frontopolar delta, theta, and combined delta-theta coherence means. Electrode-pair, regional, all-frequency, distributional, global-reference, frontopolar, and age sensitivity analyses assessed robustness.ResultsBD had higher adjusted coherence than all comparison groups across the three primary measures (partial η2 = .037-.040); Holm-adjusted BD-HC, BD-DD, and BD-SZ contrasts were significant for each measure. Features surviving false discovery rate correction were concentrated in the delta and theta bands. Findings were robust to distributional, outlier, and global-coherence analyses, but effects were strongest in frontopolar pairs and attenuated as anterior electrodes were excluded.ConclusionsBD showed higher covariate-adjusted frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp coherence than HC within this dataset. Differences from DD and SZ were smaller and concentrated in frontopolar pairs susceptible to ocular artifacts. Because only scalp-level coherence features were available and participant-level artifact-rejection data were unavailable, the findings do not establish a diagnostic biomarker, diagnostic specificity, or source-level mechanism. Artifact-controlled replication is required.

papers.title: Characterizing source-level electroencephalography activities to single-pulse TMS-EEG.
papers.abstract: To distinguish active from sham single-pulse TMS responses over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) using source-level EEG, emphasizing target-region effects and exploratory whole-brain patterns. Thirty-three healthy adults underwent active and sham TMS-EEG. We assessed local TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), electric-field simulations, and source-derived significant current density (SCD) and scattering (SCS). Target-region ROI analyses examined early (30-60 ms) and late (250-350 ms) responses; whole-brain differences were tested using cluster-based permutation tests. Peripheral EEG measures were evaluated before and after independent component analysis (ICA) and used as covariates. Active stimulation produced larger early local TEPs than sham (2.15 ± 1.39 vs. 0.85 ± 0.66 μV; Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001), a more negative N100, and a larger P200. Target-region SCS and SCD were greater with active stimulation in both windows (all adjusted p < 0.01). Whole-brain tests identified significant late SCS (275-333 ms) and SCD (269-374 and 271-366 ms) clusters, but no early clusters. Measured peripheral differences were nonsignificant after ICA. Covariate adjustment preserved the SCS and one SCD cluster, whereas the other SCD cluster was not significant after muscle-related adjustment. Target-region source measures differentiated active from sham stimulation at early and late latencies, whereas significant whole-brain clusters were observed only at late latencies. Early source-level findings complement sensor-level TEPs, but late-stage source evidence requires cautious interpretation.

papers.title: Dermal α-synuclein seeding in relation to REM sleep behavior disorder across prodromal and Parkinson disease cohorts.
papers.abstract: REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a well-established prodromal manifestation of synucleinopathy and is closely linked to peripheral clinical features in Parkinson disease (PD). Dermal α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) provides a peripheral measure of pathological α-synuclein across these disease stages. We performed a cross-sectional analysis of data from the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI), including controls, participants with polysomnography-confirmed RBD, and participants with PD. Skin SAA positivity and participant-level kinetic measures (area under the curve [AUC], maximum fluorescence [Fmax], and time to threshold [TTT]) were assessed at 1:20 and 1:50 lysate dilutions. Participants with PD were further classified as suspected brain/motor-enriched or body/peripheral-enriched based on prespecified exploratory clinical features. Skin SAA positivity was detected in 53.3% of participants with polysomnography-confirmed RBD compared with none of the controls, and RBD participants showed significantly faster amplification than controls at both lysate dilutions. Within PD, binary SAA positivity was higher in the suspected body/peripheral-enriched than brain/motor-enriched phenotype, but the difference was not statistically significant (83.3% vs 47.6%; p = 0.067). All seven kinetic measures were greater in the suspected body/peripheral-enriched phenotype after false discovery rate correction, but these differences were not retained when RBDSQ total score was removed from the classification. RBDSQ total score was the only clinical variable associated with skin SAA kinetics after correction and was significantly associated with six of the seven kinetic measures. These findings show that dermal α-synuclein seeding is detectable in PSG-confirmed prodromal RBD and is associated with RBD-related clinical features within established PD.

papers.title: A Mixed-Precision CNN-LSTM Accelerator Featuring Long-Kernel Memory Reuse and Dynamic Quantization for Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: This letter presents a mixed-precision CNN-LSTM accelerator for EEG-based sleep staging. To efficiently execute long temporal convolutions, a serpentine dataflow propagates activations between neighboring processing elements, reducing memory accesses by 6.2× and 2.25× compared with output- and weight-stationary dataflows, respectively. A hybrid quantization scheme applies runtime dynamic quantization to the LSTM and MLP layers and assigns mixed precision on a layer-by-layer basis, reducing model size by 4.16×. Combined with a bit-flexible MAC architecture and channel-grouped memory scheduling, the accelerator supports INT2/4/8/16 inference. Fabricated in 65 nm CMOS, the accelerator consumes 0.40 mW and achieves a 258× speedup over an iso-frequency 32b RISC-V processor. Evaluated across all 62 subjects in the public MASS-SS3 dataset using 31-fold leave-two-subject-out cross-validation, the mixed-precision approach with hybrid quantization maintains 5-class accuracy within 0.15% of the floating-point baseline when optimized for general sleep staging and N3 sensitivity within 0.51% when optimized for deep-sleep detection. The developed techniques are broadly applicable to EEG-based DL workloads.

papers.title: Neural Entropy Pattern : An EEG Representation for Predicting Depression Therapy Outcomes.
papers.abstract: We propose the Neural Entropy Pattern (NEP), an electroencephalography (EEG) representation intended to separate responders from non-responders before treatment. NEP consists of ten entropy measures, computed from 19 channels in five frequency bands and the broadband signal. It was used as a $20 \times 57$ image by twelve deep learning models and as a flat vector by seven shallow classifiers, and was evaluated on a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) dataset ($n = 30$) and a repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) dataset ($n = 61$) under leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) and patient-level five-fold cross-validation, with one prediction per patient and without using the held-out patients for training, early stopping or model selection. The highest balanced accuracy (BA) was, for SSRI, 76.4\% under LOSO (EfficientNet-B0; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC, 0.89) and 72.2\% under five-fold cross-validation (linear support vector machine, SVM; AUC 0.77) and, for rTMS, 62.1\% ($k$-nearest neighbours; AUC 0.62) and 63.7\% (linear SVM; AUC 0.63). These are the best of 19 models, selected post hoc (95\% confidence intervals 23--32 points). Both SSRI results were above chance by AUC (Holm-adjusted $p = 0.001$ and 0.027). Log-energy and differential entropy carried most of the Shapley-value importance (72\% for SSRI, 60\% for rTMS). For SSRI, the largest group differences were at the left fronto-temporal electrode F7 ($\delta$, $\theta$, $\beta$ and broadband domains; relatively higher power in responders), and the most important features were at F7 and T3 ($\beta$ and $\gamma$ rhythms, broadband signal); for rTMS, the most important features were at the right frontal electrode F4 ($\alpha$ rhythm, broadband signal). The NEP image performed comparably to a multichannel continuous wavelet transform image, and the NEP vector to statistical features.&#xD.

papers.title: Group-specific associations among sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and frontal alpha asymmetry in college students: evidence from a cross-sectional EEG study.
papers.abstract: Poor sleep quality is associated with depressive symptoms, but its accompanying neurophysiological correlates remain unclear in non-clinical college students. This study examined associations among sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) in students with and without elevated depressive symptoms. This cross-sectional study included 120 college students, comprising 60 students with depressive symptoms (DS) and 60 non-depressed controls (NC), classified using the Self-Rating Depression Scale. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and FAA was derived from resting-state EEG. Analyses included BMI-adjusted group comparisons, partial correlations, regression models, and an exploratory indirect-path analysis. False discovery rate correction was applied to multiple comparisons. After BMI adjustment, the DS group had higher PSQI scores [median (P25, P75): 7 (6, 10) vs. 3 (1, 5)] and lower composite FAA values [-0.041 (-0.116, 0.031) vs. 0.056 (0.017, 0.103); both p < 0.001] than the NC group. Similar FAA differences were observed using frontopolar and frontal electrode-pair indices. PSQI scores were positively correlated with depressive symptoms in both groups (DS: r = 0.412, q = 0.006; NC: r = 0.462, q = 0.001). In the DS group, composite FAA was negatively correlated with PSQI (r = -0.322, q = 0.034) and depressive symptoms (r = -0.388, q = 0.010); neither FAA-related association reached statistical significance in the NC group. After BMI adjustment, PSQI and FAA were jointly associated with depressive symptom severity in the DS group (R 2 = 0.243). An exploratory indirect-path analysis yielded an indirect association estimate of 0.092 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.002-0.202). Poorer sleep quality was associated with greater depressive symptom severity in both groups, whereas FAA-related associations were observed mainly in the DS group. These findings suggest that FAA may be a candidate neurophysiological correlate of the concurrent association between sleep quality and depressive symptoms in non-clinical college students. Causal mediation cannot be inferred from this cross-sectional study.

papers.title: Integrated roles of regulatory non-coding RNAs in circadian gene expression and disease pathogenesis.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythm (CR) is an intrinsic biological oscillation of nearly 24 h that does not merely respond to the diurnal cycle of the Earth, but rather actively anticipates it. CR can be disrupted by many environmental, physiological and behavioral factors such as irregular sleep-wake cycles, prolonged exposure to artificial light at night, shift-work schedules, altered feeding schedules, trans meridian travel, aging, psychological stress and neurodegenerative diseases. Disruption of circadian rhythm is associated with the onset of cancer, endocrine disorders, neurological complexities, and metabolic dysfunctions. Advances in RNA biology have highlighted the role of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) in regulating gene expression related to circadian rhythm. While previous studies mainly reviewed individual ncRNA classes or their roles in specific diseases like cancer, an integrative approach across multiple ncRNA categories and diseases is still elusive. This review summarizes recent progress on the roles of microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs in circadian rhythm regulation and their dysfunctions that lead to several pathological conditions. Among these transcripts, miRNAs are well-documented post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression, whereas lncRNAs and circRNAs exhibit context-specific gene regulation. Moreover, research on circular RNAs is emerging and warrants more scientific endeavors to unearth their detailed mechanisms. A holistic view of ncRNA-mediated circadian regulation will provide innovative perspectives on disease mechanisms and potentially aid in the development of targeted therapeutics that restore circadian homeostasis.

papers.title: Intermittent Hypoxia Induces Epigenetic Changes and p16-Mediated Senescence in Vascular Dysfunction in Male Mice.
papers.abstract: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is a pervasive cardiovascular risk factor linked to accelerated aging. We investigated the underlying tissue-specific and systemic epigenetic mechanisms and the role of cellular senescence in the pathophysiology of OSA and associated cardiovascular disease (CVD). C57BL/6J male mice were exposed to intermittent hypoxia (IH) or room air (RA) (n=25 mice/group) for 7 to 210 days. DNA methylation profiling was conducted on left cardiac ventricle and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and the impact of IH duration was studied using regression models. Epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) was calculated using a multi-tissue epigenetic clock. The role of p16-mediated senescence in IH-induced vascular dysfunction was assessed using transgenic mouse models (n=8 mice/group). IH exposures increased blood pressure and altered endothelial function in male mice. IH/RA differentially methylated positions (DMPs) were identified in left cardiac ventricle (n=5,747) and PBMCs (n=1,307), with minimal overlap (n=163, p=8.03 x 10-8). Both tissues differed in the EAA trajectory throughout the exposures. Epigenetic changes linked to cardiac dysfunction and cellular senescence, highlighting the Cdkn2a gene (encoding the p16 protein, a marker of cellular senescence). p16 expression was increased in aortic endothelial cells following IH. Systemic ablation of p16-expressing cells reversed IH-induced hypertension and restored coronary flow reserve. IH induces duration-dependent, tissue-specific epigenetic dysregulation and accelerated biological aging with p16-mediated cellular senescence as a primary driver. Targeting the senescent endothelium can revert OSA-induced vascular dysfunction, thereby establishing a novel mechanistic framework for cellular senescence as a therapeutic target in OSA.

papers.title: Improved sleep and clinical outcomes following a single-session intervention among adolescents with borderline personality disorder features.
papers.abstract: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a serious mental illness that often emerges in adolescence. Although efficacious treatments have been developed, they are often lengthy, expensive, inaccessible, and require specialized training to deliver. Optimizing BPD prevention and early treatment is an important public health priority. Disrupted sleep is closely linked to key BPD features, and prior research has documented a range of sleep problems among BPD samples that appear to worsen symptom course and duration. This intervention trial (NCT04507308) assessed the effects of a single-session sleep-focused treatment on adolescent sleep and BPD-related symptoms. Fifty-seven adolescents (ages 13-18) with 3+ clinically impairing BPD features and at least some self-reported sleep-related difficulties participated with a caregiver. Participants completed baseline surveys, interviews, and 10-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) protocol to examine BPD symptoms and sleep in daily life. Youth also collected at-home ambulatory electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings before undergoing the treatment informed by the Transdiagnostic Sleep and Circadian Intervention. Post-treatment, youth practiced their new sleep routine for approximately one month before undergoing reassessment (EMA, EEG, surveys). Many indices of sleep quantity and quality improved across both objective (EEG) and subjective assessments (EMA and self- and caregiver-report). Youth reported an earlier clock time at sleep onset and earlier waketime, more sleep, and fewer awakenings in daily life. Every sleep-related questionnaire score improved at post-intervention and was maintained at one-month follow-up. Multiple (though not all) indices of BPD symptoms also improved significantly. Findings suggest sleep may be a promising intervention target for at-risk youth.

papers.title: Circadian disruption worsens postseptic pulmonary fibrotic remodeling through a CLOCK/PIEZO1-linked myeloid immunometabolic program.
papers.abstract: Whether circadian rhythm disruption (CRD) promotes fibrotic remodeling after septic lung injury remains unclear. We tested whether CRD drives this process through macrophage CLOCK-PIEZO1 signaling. Lung specimens from patients with sepsis-associated lung injury and non-injured controls were analyzed alongside public murine lung transcriptomic datasets. Mice underwent cecal ligation and puncture or sham surgery and were maintained under stable or repeatedly shifted light-dark cycles; selected experiments included LysM-lineage Piezo1 deletion. Day-3 lung injury and day-28 fibrosis were assessed, and mechanisms were defined using genetic, biochemical and co-culture approaches. CRD suppressed CLOCK expression in macrophage-lineage cells, leading to increased PIEZO1 expression and aggravated collagen deposition. CLOCK repressed Piezo1 transcription through a promoter E-box. Loss of myeloid Clock reduced Clock mesor and amplitude by 66.3% and 90.3%, respectively, increased Piezo1 mesor by 54.0%, and produced genotype-by-rhythm interactions for both genes (P < 0.0001). PIEZO1 activation impaired lysosomal acid lipase (LAL)-dependent lipophagy and promoted ZDHHC19-mediated peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4) palmitoylation and extracellular-trap formation. LysM-lineage Piezo1 deletion attenuated fibrosis. PIEZO1 inhibition or DNase I reduced epithelial injury and fibroblast activation induced by extracellular DNA-rich macrophage signals. CRD promotes post-septic fibrosis through a CLOCK-PIEZO1-linked macrophage immunometabolic program, identifying PIEZO1, extracellular DNA-rich traps and impaired lipid clearance as candidate targets.

papers.title: What's in a Story? Studying Neural Narrative Engagement with Auditory Passages Using EEG Inter-Subject Correlation
papers.abstract: Narrative engagement - a state implicating attention as well as emotional and sequential processing - is crucial in contexts ranging from social interaction to education. Yet we still lack an understanding of how narrative contents and listener perceptions relate to the neural responses they elicit. In this study, we investigate relationships between auditory narratives and listener responses using electroencephalography inter-subject correlation (EEG-ISC), a measure of neural synchrony that has been shown to correlate with narrative cohesion, attention, preference, and learning. We analyzed dense-array EEG recorded from 46 adult participants who listened to social and non-social narrated literary excerpts. The data were spatially optimized using Reliable Components Analysis, and ISC was calculated for each of the three maximally reliable components (RCs) on a per-stimulus basis. While we found no significant relationships between EEG-ISC and broad social/non-social categorizations of the excerpts, ISC for high sociocognitive word usage significantly exceeded that of medium and low word usage in the third spatial component, RC3. We further observed a significant positive correlation between participants' summed ratings of interest, compulsion, and enjoyment and ISC, both for RC2 and when summed across RC1-RC3. Interaction analyses suggest that passage content and behavioral responses contributed independently as additive effects to these relationships. Taken together, these findings extend previous research utilizing EEG-ISC in natural speech contexts and, importantly, suggest that the decomposition of EEG into maximally correlated spatial components can separate co-occurring neural processes engaged during story listening.

papers.title: Circadian Regulation of Gastrointestinal Physiology and Disease: Mechanisms, Chrononutrition, and Therapeutic Opportunities.
papers.abstract: Gastrointestinal physiology varies across the 24-h day as central and peripheral clocks coordinate metabolism, epithelial renewal, mucosal immunity, barrier permeability, motility, and microbial activity. Disrupted temporal organization is associated with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma. This narrative review integrates molecular mechanisms with clinical evidence, distinguishing experimental causality from observational associations. Chrononutrition examines interactions between eating patterns and circadian biology, including meal timing, frequency, regularity, and eating-window duration. Human studies support effects of meal timing on peripheral rhythms, but improvements in metabolic markers do not consistently exceed those achieved by calorie restriction. Sleep disturbance predicts disease activity in some inflammatory bowel disease cohorts, whereas preliminary sleep-intervention trials have not established prevention of relapse. Chronomodulated chemotherapy illustrates both potential benefits and implementation barriers, including sex-dependent outcomes and the need for programmable infusion systems. Chronotype, an individual's preference for earlier or later sleep and activity, may modify the feasibility of temporal interventions. Translation requires adequately controlled trials that assess biological phase, disease activity, nutritional safety, adherence, and clinically meaningful outcomes alongside standard care.

papers.title: Clinical outcomes and EEG monitoring in absence epilepsy trials: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Absence epilepsy is characterized by typical absence seizures with distinct electroclinical signatures. The main semiological feature is sudden behavioral arrest associated with brief impairment of consciousness, and the electroencephalographic (EEG) hallmark pattern is generalized, symmetric 2.5-4 Hz spike-and-wave discharges (GSW). Absence epilepsy diagnosis relies on correlating GSW with observable clinical manifestations. Monitoring therapeutic effects based solely on reported symptoms may be misleading, as behavioral arrest can be difficult to identify. Patients often do not recall most seizures, and observable motor/behavioral signs may be subtle, such as minimal twitches or transient lapses in responsiveness, which may go unnoticed. In clinical trials for absence epilepsies, quantification of GSW activity by EEG offers an objective and accurate measure of electrical burden and therapeutic efficacy. Despite technological limitations, GSW remains a robust neurophysiological endpoint. Increasing evidence indicates that the timing and burden of GSW correlate with epilepsy comorbidities, including attention, cognition, behavior, and sleep. We reviewed the published literature regarding GSW as an outcome measure in absence epilepsy, including nonseizure outcomes and comorbidities. Our review highlights (1) nearly 100% of clinical absence seizures exhibit sustained GSW discharges on EEG; (2) >49% of electrographic seizures are asymptomatic, indicating that reliance on seizure diaries without EEG monitoring underestimates seizure frequency and burden; (3) Genetic Generalized Epilepsy is not a benign condition and is associated with a high prevalence of cognitive and behavioral comorbidities, supporting evaluation beyond clinically observable seizures and the use of prolonged (≥24-h) EEG monitoring; (4) circadian and multidien cycles further emphasize the need for prolonged EEG recordings to reduce timing-related bias; and (5) antiseizure medications effective in absence epilepsy reduce GSW, supporting EEG monitoring as an objective treatment outcome measure. We therefore recommend incorporating ≥24-h EEG in future clinical trials, especially in (young) adults, and exploring comorbidities as important outcome measures. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Absence epilepsy causes brief episodes in which a person suddenly stops what they are doing and may not be aware of their surroundings. Many of these seizures have no obvious signs and are often missed or forgotten, meaning seizure diaries alone do not show the full picture. Our review shows that brain recordings (electroencephalographic, EEG), especially when done over 24 h or longer, detect many unrecognized seizures and better measure how well treatments work. EEG findings are also linked to problems with attention, thinking, behavior, and sleep, highlighting the need to look beyond visible seizures when evaluating treatments in clinical trials.

papers.title: Sleep deprivation remodels hepatic immune microenvironment via circadian gene dysregulation and promotes hepatocellular carcinoma progression.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) is a widespread public health issue that may adversely affect liver health. Although SD is a recognized circadian stressor, the mechanisms linking circadian rhythm-related changes to liver injury remain poorly understood. This study aims to systematically investigate the role of circadian rhythm-related genes (CRGs) in mediating SD-induced remodeling of the liver immune microenvironment and its potential implications for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Transcriptomic datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) following SD. A rat SD model was used to assess hepatic injury via serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Functional enrichment analyses and machine learning identified pivotal CRGs. Key genes were validated across datasets and in HCC. Immune infiltration was analyzed using CIBERSORT and the Tumor Immune Estimation Resource (TIMER) database. Experimental validation in a rat SD model demonstrated significant elevations in serum ALT and AST levels, confirming the induction of hepatic injury. SD induced significant alterations in CRGs. CRGs were found to centrally regulate inflammatory, immune, and oncogenic processes. A machine learning framework identified six core CRGs (Cirbp, Srebf1, Fbxo31, Hsp90aa1, Btc, and Dlgap1), whose dysregulated expression was consistently validated. Furthermore, SD led to a significant reshuffling of the hepatic immune landscape, characterized by changes in five distinct immune cell types, which showed strong correlations with the six key CRGs. Notably, among the six hub CRGs, Cirbp and Hsp90aa1 were significantly associated with immune infiltration levels and prognosis in HCC patients. In addition, Serpine1, which was independently identified by LASSO as a key SD-related gene, showed similar associations.

papers.title: Analysis of nighttime heart rate variability during rapid eye movement and non-rapid eye movement in OSA.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a heterogeneous condition. However, many inconsistencies remain regarding the analysis of heart rate variability (HRV) and autonomic nervous system (ANS) function differences among patients with rapid eye movement (REM)-related OSA, nonrapid eye movement (NREM)-related OSA during different sleep periods. This retrospective study included 373 patients with OSA who completed polysomnography (PSG) at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University from May 2023 to February 2024. Patients were classified into REM-related OSA (REM-OSA), NREM-related OSA (NREM-OSA), and non-stage-specific OSA groups according to PSG. Clinical demographics, PSG parameters, and HRV indices were compared across the three groups. Multivariable regression models were constructed to examine the independent associations of AHI and OSA phenotype with HRV, adjusting for age, gender, BMI, and segment duration. A total of 373 OSA patients were included (120 REM-OSA, 90 NREM-OSA, and 163 non-stage-specific OSA). In female patients with mild-to-moderate OSA, no significant differences in HRV were observed across the three phenotypes. In male patients with mild-to-moderate OSA, the REM-OSA group exhibited lower LFnu and LF/HF and higher HFnu during N1 and N2 sleep compared with the other phenotypes. During REM sleep, the REM-OSA group showed higher SDNN than the NREM-OSA group. In patients with severe OSA, the non-stage-specific group showed lower SDNN, RMSSD, and pNN50 during REM sleep than the NREM-OSA group. Multivariate regression showed that AHI was significantly associated with frequency-domain HRV indices across all sleep stages. After adjusting for age, gender, BMI, and segment duration, the REM-OSA phenotype was independently associated with lower LFnu and LF/HF and higher HFnu during N1 and N2 sleep, but not during REM sleep (explaining 8.6%-24.7% of variance). The autonomic effects of REM-OSA are sex-dependent and severity-dependent. In male patients with mild-to-moderate OSA, the REM-OSA phenotype was associated with relative parasympathetic dominance during N1 and N2 sleep, but not during REM sleep. ANS function may not be the primary mechanism linking REM-OSA to cardiovascular risk, and the autonomic profile of REM-OSA is more nuanced than previously recognized.

papers.title: Rituximab-responsive epilepsia partialis continua in autoimmune Polyendocrine syndrome: A video-EEG-EMG polygraphic study.
papers.abstract: Epilepsia partialis continua (EPC) is a rare and challenging form of focal motor status epilepticus. Its occurrence strictly in systemic autoimmune disorders without overt encephalitis is exceptional. Corticosteroids are first-line therapy but may be limited by significant side effects and poor metabolic tolerability. We report a 54-year-old woman with Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome (APS), including autoimmune hepatitis, latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, celiac disease, and hypothyroidism, presenting with continuous jerks of right III-V fingers. Neurological examination showed continuous, irregular jerks confined to the right III, IV, and V fingers. Extensive serum and CSF screenings, including neuronal antibodies, and MRI were unremarkable. Ictal HMPAO-SPECT revealed a focal hyperperfusion in the left hand-knob area of the primary motor cortex. Brain FDG-PET revealed focal hypometabolism in the same region. Video-EEG-EMG polygraphy showed intermittent spikes and polyspikes over the left central region preceding EMG bursts of the right V finger's abductor muscle with a latency of approximately 30-40 ms. These findings were consistent with EPC. Corticosteroids induced marked improvement but were discontinued due to severe glycemic worsening. Subsequent treatment with oral steroids, IVIG, and multiple antiseizure medications were ineffective. Administration of Rituximab led to complete and sustained clinical and electrophysiological remission, which persisted at the 18-month follow-up. EPC can be a severe, focal manifestation of systemic autoimmunity even without encephalitis. Rituximab represents an effective steroid-sparing option for refractory autoimmune EPC, particularly in metabolically vulnerable patients.

papers.title: Depressive symptoms moderate daily anticipated and momentary emotion dynamics and associate with complex brain network topology: Resting-state EEG and ecological momentary assessment evidence.
papers.abstract: The dynamic linkage between anticipated and momentary emotion is a core daily regulatory process, yet the psychopathological and neurophysiological mechanisms disrupting this linkage in depression remain unclear. By bridging macroscopic neural topology with microscopic behavioral dynamics, this study investigated the within-person dynamics of these emotions and their cross-level associations with depressive symptoms and brain network topology. Integrating resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA; 3 assessments/day), we recruited 96 young adults. Minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis was applied to characterize baseline brain network topology across multiple frequency bands. Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) was employed to examine within-person dynamics and cross-level statistical moderation. Anticipated emotion prospectively predicted subsequent momentary positive emotion (β = .191) and inversely predicted momentary negative emotion (β = -.125). However, baseline depressive symptoms significantly moderated this prospective affective dynamic: Johnson-Neyman analyses identified empirical transition ranges (PHQ-9 scores 5.7-9.7; mild symptom range) beyond which the prospective emotional link attenuated to non-significance. Furthermore, topological metrics in the theta and delta bands exhibited indirect statistical associations with daily emotional dynamics via their cross-sectional relationship with baseline depressive symptoms. An attenuated prospective association between positive anticipation and subsequent momentary emotional experience represents a key affective alteration in depressive distress. This daily emotional attenuation co-occurs with elevated depressive distress and is indirectly associated with a centralized topological organization in low-frequency resting-state brain networks. These findings provide novel neurophysiological indicators and highlight the critical window for ecological interventions before symptom severity reaches the moderate range.

papers.title: Sleep Deprivation, Occupational Stress, and Work-related Determinants of Sleep Disturbance Among Practicing Physicians: A Cross-sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation and occupational stress are increasingly recognized as critical determinants of physician well-being, with potential implications for healthcare quality and patient safety. However, data on sleep patterns and their determinants among heterogeneous groups of practicing physicians remain limited. To assess sleep patterns, lifestyle characteristics, and work-related stressors among practicing physicians and to examine their interrelationships. This cross-sectional, survey-based study was conducted between January and March 2026 among practicing physicians using an anonymous, self-administered electronic questionnaire. A total of 627 physicians participated. Data collected included demographic and professional characteristics, work patterns, lifestyle behaviors, sleep-related parameters, and perceived stress. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data. Among 627 physicians, 54.1% reported sleeping ≤6 h per night, and 51.9% experienced sleep disturbance at least twice per week. Nearly one-third (28.3%) reported working more than 60 h per week. Stress negatively affected sleep in 48.5% of respondents. The most common contributors to sleep disruption were anxiety or stress (44.2%) and patient emergencies (31.9%), while key work-related stressors included poor work-life balance (40.5%), administrative burden (36.5%), and high patient load (32.5%). Despite these findings, most physicians reported low tobacco and alcohol use and moderate levels of physical activity. Sleep deprivation and sleep disturbance are highly prevalent among practicing physicians and are strongly associated with work-related stressors rather than lifestyle factors. These findings highlight the need for system-level interventions targeting workload, scheduling, and workplace stress to improve physician sleep health and overall well-being.

papers.title: Exploring the genetic determinants of ALS in a North Indian cohort using a genomic screening approach
papers.abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a clinically and genetically heterogenous neurodegenerative disorder in which both monogenic and complex genetic mechanism contribute to disease susceptibility. Increasing evidence also indicates that non motor manifestations, including sleep disturbances, significantly influence disease burden. This study aimed to characterize the genetic spectrum of ALS in a predominantly North Indian cohort while evaluating the prevalence of sleep related abnormalities. Methods: Seventy-three clinically diagnosed ALS patients were recruited from a tertiary care centre in North India. Disease severity was assessed using the ALSFRS-R. Sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and REM sleep behaviour disorder symptoms were evaluated using the PSQI, ESS and RBDQ questionnaires, respectively. Genetic analysis included targeted sequencing of SOD1, TARDBP, and ANG, followed by repeat expansion analysis of C9orf72, ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3, and ATXN7. Whole exome sequencing was performed in selected cases to further investigate the genetic basis of ALS. Results: The cohort demonstrated a male predominance and an earlier age of onset compared to many Western populations. Poor sleep quality and excessive daytime sleepiness were frequently observed although no significant association was found between sleep parameters and disease severity. Genetic screening identified a pathogenic/likely pathogenic TARDBP variant classified by ClinVar while no known or novel pathogenic variants were detected in SOD1 or ANG. Repeat expansion studies revealed one patient harbouring pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions. For the ATXN1, one patient harboured pathogenic repeat expansions and two patients carried intermediate length repeats. Additionally, one patient harboured intermediate repeat expansions in ATXN2. Whole exome sequencing revealed novel and rare variants in ALS associated genes including ANXA11, SIGMAR1, SETX, ERBB4 and NEK1, highlighting substantial genetic heterogeneity. Conclusions: Our findings highlight the complex genetic heterogeneity of ALS, with pathogenic repeat expansions and rare variants identified across multiple disease associated genes. These results demonstrate the importance of comprehensive genetic testing to improve the detection of clinically relevant variants in ALS. In addition, the high prevalence of sleep related disturbances observed in the cohort emphasizes the need to incorporate non motor assessment into routine clinical evaluation of patients with ALS.

papers.title: Epilepsy Surgery in Patients with Non-Lesional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Evaluated with Stereoelectroencephalography: Retrospective Analysis in a High-Complexity Center and Literature Review.
papers.abstract: Background and objective When epilepsy is associated with non-lesional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and there is no anatomical-electro-clinical correlation of seizures, invasive studies, such as stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG), are necessary to determine the epileptogenic zone (EZ) and, subsequently, the type of surgery to be performed. The aim of this work is to report the results of epilepsy surgery in patients with non-lesional MRI evaluated with SEEG and to conduct a literature review. Materials and methods Retrospective descriptive observational study. Non-invasive pre-surgical studies included neuropsychological and psychiatric evaluation, MRI with epilepsy protocol, positron emission tomography, and video-electroencephalography. Invasive studies included SEEG. Surgery was performed with curative intent in all patients. The Engel criteria were used to evaluate post-surgical results. Pathological anatomy and its correlation with surgical outcomes were considered. Results Eleven patients met the inclusion criteria for our analysis. All presented with inconsistent non-invasive preoperative examinations that did not allow for localization of the epileptic zone (EZ). SEEG was performed, successfully theorizing the ZE according to the electroclinical hypothesis in all patients. Four patients underwent anterior temporal lobectomy and seven underwent extratemporal corticectomy. We obtained a 63.6% rate of good postoperative results. Conclusion The SEEG allowed theorizing the ZE in all patients. The overall postoperative results were consistent with the literature. However, in the subgroup analysis, unlike previous studies, in our case series, extratemporal non-lesional epilepsy showed better postoperative results than temporal non-lesional epilepsy.

papers.title: Vestibular Epilepsy Presenting With Isolated Recurrent Vertigo and Postictal Headache: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Vestibular epilepsy, also referred to as epileptic vertigo syndrome, is a rare and underrecognized cause of recurrent episodic vertigo. Currently, there are no universally accepted diagnostic criteria for vestibular epilepsy. A 38-year-old woman presented with an eight-month history of recurrent spontaneous episodes of rotational vertigo lasting one to two minutes and occurring multiple times daily. Episodes were accompanied by nausea and vomiting and were followed by bilateral throbbing headaches. Neurological examination, bedside vestibular assessment, and cognitive screening were unremarkable. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated no structural epileptogenic lesion, while brainstem evoked response audiometry was normal. Electroencephalography revealed frequent generalized epileptiform discharges with a photoparoxysmal response during intermittent photic stimulation. The patient was diagnosed with vestibular epilepsy with postictal headache after exclusion of alternative causes of episodic vertigo. Treatment with extended-release divalproex sodium resulted in a marked reduction in attack frequency and improvement in symptoms during follow-up. Vestibular epilepsy represents an uncommon seizure manifestation in which vestibular symptoms predominate and may occur in isolation. In this patient, the brief stereotyped attacks, normal brain neuroimaging, absence of peripheral vestibular abnormalities, epileptiform electroencephalographic findings, and favorable response to antiseizure therapy supported the diagnosis. In cases of recurrent episodic vertigo presenting concurrently with headache, vestibular epilepsy remains a diagnostic challenge, mainly because overt neurological manifestations are often absent. Recent literature suggests that electroencephalography should be considered in patients with recurrent unexplained brief vertigo, particularly when episodes are stereotyped or resistant to conventional vestibular therapies.

papers.title: Changes in negative affect and resting-state EEG power following an EEG-derived generative reality art experience: a pilot pre-post study.
papers.abstract: Physiological signals are increasingly incorporated into personalized immersive media, but little is known about affective and neurophysiological changes when such signals are used as artistic material. This exploratory pilot study examined an electroencephalography (EEG)-derived generative virtual reality (VR) art experience in which participant-specific EEG signals were symbolically transformed into prompts for immersive visual environments. Thirty healthy university students completed the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule and resting-state EEG recordings before and after a single 5-min experience. EEG analyses examined log-transformed absolute alpha- and beta-band power across frontal, frontocentral, and central regions, with false discovery rate correction. Negative affect decreased from pre- to post-experience (mean change = -3.13, FDR-adjusted p = 0.004), whereas positive affect did not change significantly. Absolute beta-band power decreased across all three regions, and absolute alpha-band power decreased in the frontocentral and central regions (FDR-adjusted p values ≤0.022). Exploratory relative-power analyses showed no significant pre-post differences after correction for multiple comparisons. Frontal alpha asymmetry did not change significantly. Changes in EEG measures were not significantly associated with changes in affect after correction for multiple comparisons. The EEG findings therefore do not establish a neural mechanism for the reduction in negative affect. These findings indicate that the experience was associated with short-term changes in negative affect and resting-state spectral power. Because this pilot study used a single-group design, the findings do not establish causality or therapeutic efficacy. Instead, they provide an initial empirical basis for controlled research on physiological data as personalized material for immersive art and affective experience.

papers.title: The regenerative hexagon: six domains shaping musculoskeletal regenerative outcomes.
papers.abstract: The classical regenerative triad of scaffold, cells, and growth factors has guided musculoskeletal regenerative medicine for over two decades, yet outcome variability after orthobiologic treatment is not explained by preparation parameters alone. Contemporary regenerative biology already recognizes that host immunity, mechanics, and metabolism shape repair; what is less developed is a framework that integrates these dimensions for orthobiologic treatment and states their interactions in testable form. We propose an update of the triad concept rather than a replacement of it: a Regenerative Hexagon that retains the three construct components and adds three host-state domains that modify the response to them. These are the Systemic Host Environment, encompassing the gut-joint axis, sleep, medications, conditioning, metabolic status, and the pre-existing immune profile; Biomechanics and Mechanotransduction; and Cellular Energetics, defined as the energetic and redox state of resident and administered cells, which biophysical modalities are proposed to modify. Six short diagonals connect non-adjacent vertices, forming two interlocking triads that generate the Regenerative Star, and the framework is read as a sequence of states across the phases of repair rather than as a static configuration. The evidence for each component is graded with explicit criteria, and interactions demonstrated within a single experimental system are separated from those inferred from separate literatures. Convergent mechanisms are proposed: sleep fragmentation in healthy volunteers and dysbiosis-derived endotoxin in mechanistic studies both engage Toll-like receptor 4 signalling, and host metabolic burden was associated with orthobiologic response in a preparation-dependent manner. We hypothesize that the pillars interact multiplicatively rather than additively, a proposition not yet supported by a quantitative model and testable in factorial trials. The Regenerative Star is offered as a hypothesis-generating framework rather than a validated clinical instrument, reorienting inquiry from which preparation is superior toward in which host a given preparation performs.
